```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(zupmxode)
```

We take one model from text to a simulated population: compile it, give
it a week of doses, solve it for one subject, simulate a hundred, and
evaluate one subject the way an estimator does. By the end you will know
the package's four objects (a model, an event table, a solution and a
prepared subject) and the functions that make them. How fast this is, and
where it runs, is left to the
[Performance and platforms](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zupmxode/articles/performance.html)
article.

## Compile a model

A **model** is written in rxode2's syntax and read by R's own parser, so
an rxode2 model in the supported subset runs unchanged. This one has a
depot, a central compartment, and three parameters with a random effect
each. Compiling it takes milliseconds and no C compiler.

```{r}
m <- pmx_ode_model({
  ka <- exp(tka + eta.ka); cl <- exp(tcl + eta.cl); v <- exp(tv + eta.v)
  d/dt(depot)   <- -ka * depot
  d/dt(central) <-  ka * depot - cl / v * central
  cp <- central / v
})
m
```

`pmx_ode_info()` says what the compiler found: the compartments, the
parameters, which solver the model takes and why, and its tier.

```{r}
pmx_ode_info(m)
```

## Describe the doses

An **event table** holds NONMEM-style records: doses, and the times to
report. Here it is a week of daily 100 mg doses into the depot, observed
every hour. A data frame with NONMEM's columns (`ID`, `TIME`, `AMT`,
`CMT`, `EVID`, `MDV` and the rest) works the same way.

```{r}
ev <- pmx_ode_events(amt = 100, ii = 24, addl = 6, cmt = "depot",
                      time = seq(0, 168, by = 1))
head(ev, 3)
```

## Solve one subject

`pmx_ode_solve()` is the deterministic core: every parameter in, the
compartments and outputs at each observation out, with no random draws.
Look for `cp` rising after each dose and settling into a daily cycle.

```{r}
p <- c(tka = 0.5, tcl = 1, tv = 3, eta.ka = 0, eta.cl = 0, eta.v = 0)
out <- pmx_ode_solve(m, ev, params = p)
out[c(1, 2, 25, 26, 169), ]
```

The mistake new users make most is to leave a parameter out. The error
names it rather than solving with a default:

```{r, error = TRUE}
pmx_ode_solve(m, ev, params = c(tka = 0.5, tcl = 1, tv = 3))
```

## Simulate a population, reproducibly

`pmx_ode_sim()` draws each subject's etas from `omega` and adds residual
error to the outputs `sigma` names. Every draw is made in R with R's
random number generator, so the same seed gives the same result at any
number of threads.

```{r}
old <- pmx_ode_threads(2)
set.seed(1)
sim <- pmx_ode_sim(m, ev, theta = c(tka = 0.5, tcl = 1, tv = 3),
                    omega = diag(c(0.1, 0.1, 0.1)),
                    sigma = list(cp = prop(0.1)), n = 100)
pmx_ode_threads(old)
head(sim[c("id", "time", "cp", "cp_obs", "eta.ka", "eta.cl", "eta.v")])
```

The etas are the parameters `omega` names, or, as here, the model's
parameters named `eta...` in order. Residual error comes from `add()`,
`prop()`, their sum `add() + prop()`, or `lnorm()`; the observation with
error sits next to the prediction as `cp_obs`.

## Evaluate one subject for an estimator

An estimator tries thousands of parameter vectors on the same data. It
prepares the subjects once with `pmx_ode_subjects()`, which splits the
model's parameters into theta and eta, and then asks
`pmx_ode_subject_eval()` for one **prepared subject's** predictions and
residual variances at each vector.

```{r}
subs <- pmx_ode_subjects(m, ev)
attr(subs, "eta")
r <- pmx_ode_subject_eval(m, subs[[1]], theta = c(tka = 0.5, tcl = 1, tv = 3),
                          eta = c(eta.ka = 0, eta.cl = 0.2, eta.v = 0),
                          sigma = list(cp = prop(0.1)))
head(cbind(time = r$time, pred = r$pred, var = r$var), 3)
```

The predictions are the doubles `pmx_ode_solve()` gives for the same
parameters. The same call exists in C, for estimators written there,
through the header `inst/include/zupmxode.h`.

## Choose the solver and the tier

The solver is the most specific one the model allows (closed form, matrix
exponential, or a general ODE solver), and the tier is native code unless
the platform cannot run it. Both can be overridden; each override returns
a new model and leaves `m` as it was.

```{r}
pmx_ode_method(pmx_ode_method(m, "lsoda"))
pmx_ode_tier(pmx_ode_tier(m, "interp"))
```
